sn56.11:1.1: This is the Buddha’s first discourse proper. In the narrative following the Buddha’s awakening ([pli-tv-kd1:6.16.9]()), it follows the apparently fruitless encounter with Upaka on the road from Bodhgaya to Varanasi ([mn26:25.1](), and precedes the teaching on not-self ([sn22.59]()). It is included in full in the later treatise the Paṭisambhidāmagga ([ps2.6:1.1]()), and is alluded to many times in the Suttas, sometimes by name ([mn141:32.1]()), sometimes implicitly ([mn26:29.1]()). It is still a key text in Theravāda Buddhism, and is regularly memorized and recited. The Saṅgha at the Deer Park recite it every night.
sn56.11:1.2: These are the ascetics with whom the Bodhisatta practiced before rejecting their path of extreme asceticism ([mn36:20.2]()). The Buddha has traveled especially to teach them out of gratitude, because they were very helpful to him ([mn26:24.5]()). Their names are listed in the Vinaya account: Koṇḍañña, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahānāma, and Assaji ([pli-tv-kd1:6.31.6]()). | Note that he calls them “mendicants”, a term typically reserved for Buddhist renunciates. For a similar usage, see [mn140:3.4](). In the Vinaya account, they ordained after this teaching.
sn56.11:2.3: The Buddha begins by finding common ground with the ascetics—the rejection of sensual pleasures, repudiating their idea that he had given himself up to luxury (see [dn29:23.2.]()). Only then does he reject the five ascetics’ own practice of self-mortification. The descriptions in the Suttas make it clear that these practices were closely allied to the Jains, although the Buddha does not formally identify them ([mn85:10.2]()).
sn56.11:4.4: This definition clarifies two common misunderstandings. First, not all desire causes suffering, for some kinds of desire lead out of suffering ([sn51.15:4.1]()). Second, rebirth is not a tangential part of the Buddha’s teachings, uncritically inherited from cultural suppositions; it is baked into the fundamental meaning of the four noble truths. | The idiom _tatratatra_ (literally “there, there”) is not selective (“here and there”) but distributive (“each and every place”, “everywhere”). By taking pleasure in sense experience, the mind binds itself to the need for continued stimulation in future lives. The distancing sense “there” is important, for craving does not merely satisfy itself with what it currently experiences, but must always seek out renewed gratification. For an Upaniṣadic precursor, see the note to the same idiom at [mn2:8.8]().
sn56.11:4.5: Craving for sensual pleasures in this life or the next, binding oneself to a form that can experience such pleasures. In Buddhism, this includes not only the human realm, but all of the heavenly realms too, so far as the Brahmā realm. When a person has good kamma, they are reborn in a realm where they enjoy such pleasures, if not, in a lower realm. | Craving to continue existence (_bhavataṇhā_) refers to any desire, whether conscious or not, to continue existence after death. When it solidifies as a view it is called eternalism, and motivates religious and spiritual practices aiming at “eternal life”. As such, it especially applies to rebirth in the Brahmā realms. However, it is still present even in those who do not ascribe to such a view; craving is more primal than view (see [sn12.2:6.3]() and notes). | Craving for nonexistence is the longing to destroy the self, in contrast with the Buddhist perspective that the self is a false construct. When it crystallizes as a view it is called annihilationism.
sn56.11:4.7: These are all terms for Nibbāna.
sn56.11:4.10: Thus the four noble truths include the eightfold noble path as the final factor, just as the noble eightfold path includes the four nobles truths as its first factor, right view. They are different perspectives on the same thing.
sn56.11:9.1: The related passage at AN 8.64 suggests that the tiparivaṭṭaṁ dvādasākāraṁ apply to the knowledge, not the truths.
